title: Be holy (Leviticus 19)
hookLine: be holy, and thou shalt love thy friend as thyself, and leave gleanings for the poor

lines: THE BOOK PEOPLE GIVE UP ON.
cards: Leviticus has a reputation. It's where people who promise to read the whole Bible quietly give up: sacrifices, skin diseases, which animals you can eat.
Then chapter nineteen opens with a command that sounds enormous: "Be ye holy, because I the Lord your God am holy." You'd expect what follows to be about the temple, or incense, or long prayers.
Instead it's about farming, and wages, and how you treat a deaf man and a blind man. Holiness, it turns out, happens in a wheat field.

teach.b: First, the word. Holy, in Hebrew kadosh, means set apart, different, belonging to God. The plural, kedoshim, is how the chapter begins, and Jewish tradition still names this section of Leviticus by that word.

teach.h: LEAVE THE CORNERS OF THE FIELD.
teach.b: Second, the corners. When you reap your field, God says, don't harvest all the way to the edges or go back for the stalks you dropped. Don't strip your vineyard bare or pick up the grapes that fell.
Leave them for the poor and the stranger. The edges of your field aren't fully yours. Jewish law still keeps this as peah, the corner, with a whole section of the Mishnah devoted to it.
Later in the Bible, a poor foreign widow named Ruth will survive by gathering exactly these leftovers. Third, the list. Pay your worker the same day.
Don't curse the deaf, and don't put a stumbling block in front of the blind. Stand up for the old.
Use honest weights in the market. Love the stranger as yourself, because you were strangers in Egypt. And in the middle of it all, the line Jesus will later call the second great commandment.
The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, says: "Thou shalt love thy friend as thyself." Most English Bibles say neighbor; the Hebrew word, rea, can mean either. Fourth, what the Church draws from it.
The Second Vatican Council taught that every baptized person, not only priests and nuns, is called to holiness.
Leviticus nineteen shows what that looks like at ground level: in the paycheck, the market, the harvest, and what you leave at the edges for someone else.

how: The Second Vatican Council's Lumen Gentium teaches the universal call to holiness, and many Catholic parishes run food pantries and collections for the poor; some Catholic groups also organize gleaning on farms after the harvest.

o: spending your days in church and prayer
set apart, living as one who belongs to God
being perfect and never making mistakes

games.q: what's inside the chapter — tap the pairs.
p: the corner left for the poor
will live on what the reapers leave

s: Leviticus 19 is mostly about temple ritual
after be ye holy, it turns to harvests, wages, the deaf, the blind and honest weights.
the Douay-Rheims says love thy friend where most English Bibles say neighbor
it follows the Latin; the Hebrew rea can mean either.
the love-your-neighbor command first appears in the Gospels

games.q: you're a farmer in ancient Israel at harvest time. you've reached the edge of your field, and some stalks have fallen behind the reapers. what does Leviticus tell you to do?
o: harvest every last stalk: it's your field.
leave the corners and the fallen grain for the poor and the stranger.
sell the leftovers cheaply at market.
games.why: leave the edges unreaped and don't go back for what fell. it's for the poor and the stranger. holiness, here, is what you leave behind.

practice: Think about your own fields: your paycheck, your pantry, your time, the last slice of something, and find one corner you usually harvest right to the edge.

Picture leaving it instead: a bag for the food pantry, a generous tip, ten minutes for someone else, the last good seat. If you pray, offer that corner to God; if not, simply picture who might find it.

wordCard.voice: Be holy. The command that opens Leviticus nineteen, lived out in fields, wages, and the corners left for the poor. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: holy ones. the chapter's first command, be holy, and the name of this section of Leviticus.

carryVoice: Your line: leave the corners. What's left at the edges feeds someone else. That's day three hundred eighty-two.
